title: Programming applies to your training whether you like it or not
summary: NH argues that anyone following a routine is already programming, so lifters should learn to do it well. He says bodybuilding undervalues programming compared with powerlifting and weightlifting, and urges people to write their own programs, since even failed self-written programs teach more than outsourced ones.

claims.claim: Unless you pick exercises at random at the gym, any routine you follow is a program; programming isn't an intellectual elite term.
His gains and physique development tracked directly with his ability to program; his programs from nine years ago versus now are night and day.
Anything works for novices, so simple programs are fine at first; as you advance it becomes a game of inches and programming matters.
Powerlifting and weightlifting have made programming an art, while the bodybuilding community undervalues it, which gives bodybuilders a caveman image.
Building a physique is as much an art as posing or presentation, so physique athletes should be at the forefront of programming.
Write your own program: it should reflect who you are, and even a subpar self-written program teaches you more through failure than one written by a professional.
If you train for 10 years, you've been running programs for 10 years, so you may as well know how to write them; otherwise you're doing things without knowing what they do.
A small change in a program can turn a weak body part into a strong one, or the reverse.
All methods can work, even suboptimal ones; having no method is itself a method.
